# AI Usage Policy

We only use generative AI technologies responsibly and in accordance with SAAS’s
academic integrity and acceptable technology use policies. Check the [Student/Family Handbook](https://www.seattleacademy.org/fs/resource-manager/view/a893d109-f384-4b79-9a3d-285b962bb16f) for more information.

In short, don’t use AI to write your code. You can use it to try to explain and understand existing code, but try to understand things on your own first. Ask us for permission if you think there might be an exception.

If you are curious, here are some more details on our policies: we follow the Fedora Foundation’s [guidelines on AI-generated code](https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/council/policy/ai-contribution-policy/). If you get permission to use AI, clearly cite all your commits assisted by generative AI like this: “Assisted-By: \[AI Name\]” at the end of your message. For example, if I used ChatGPT to fix a bug with path following, I might write “Fix path following by enabling brake mode. Assisted-by: ChatGPT.”

# GitHub Development

These are the steps to developing any feature, fixing any bug, contributing any documentation, or tuning any existing capabilities.

1. Create a branch to work on your changes. We only commit directly to the main branch during stages like early repository setup and late-stage testing, when the robot will soon be on the field.

![][image1]

2. Develop all your features. Working with a partner at some point in this process is recommended, especially if this will change the robot functionality.

3. If your changes alter robot functionality, test your changes.

   1. First, develop a testing plan noting what you changed, what behavior you expect, how you will measure your result, and how you might diagnose any problems that arise

   2. Follow the [safety protocol]() for testing the robot. Use your testing plan to be efficient.

   3. Be mindful of how much time you have

   4. Make necessary adjustments



**Review Process:**

4. Merge main into your branch if it’s out of date – ask people who wrote conflicting code if you have a merge conflict you don’t know how to handle.

   **![][image2]**

5. Create a Pull Request (PR) to move your changes into the “main” branch.

   **![][image3]**
6. Ask a teammate to review your code. If you have to make any changes, ask them again once you have.

7. Ask a Programming Leader to review your PR. Update your code if necessary;

8. Merge main into your branch again if it has updated.

9. Merge the PR

# Gotchas

* Renaming files in a way that only changes case (capitalization) causes linker errors
  * Windows is a case insensitive filesystem and git will not see the change
* Always specifically define double literals. This can be done by including a decimal point (ex, 0.0) or with the d suffix (but this is ugly and really lets not start using this)

# Version Control {#version-control}

| This activity will introduce you to Git and GitHub, the version control system we use for all programming done on this team. If you are already familiar with Git and GitHub, you can ski/p this standard, as long as you share your repository with Aceius. |
| :---- |

Good Afternoon. Today, we will be covering the basics of how to use Git through GitHub, and the Kinematics object. Please make sure you have completed [002 XRP FUNDAMENTALS](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/18N1jZm_BHMhBcXJI3x58UiodouddWGEtE0DsbjtKG4o/edit) before starting this activity.

Note: If you are already familiar with Git, you may skip these first few sections. If you prefer a more visual style of learning, take a look at these slides: [GitHub 101](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PZCwb8cU917Vp-RgrtmLP9o5tAnM7Sc2hBGpRp1oULE/edit?usp=sharing)

## Git {#git}

Git is a ‘distributed version control system’. Another way to think about git is as a time machine for your projects (called repositories by git). Sometimes, your work will blow up, but with git, you can travel back in time to a working version (commit). Thus, it is called a version control system. It can work with any project type \- you can use it to store notes, essays, or even art projects. However, git is best suited to tracking text files, such as the .java files we use to store robot code.

Now, git is not just any VCS \- it is also distributed. This means you can use it to seamlessly collaborate with your peers on a project. In order to take advantage of this ability, we must register with a remote. The remote we are using is GitHub. You can [sign up for GitHub here](https://github.com/signup) (the process is fairly standard).

After this, you should download a git client for your computer. You may use any client, but we recommend and only support [GitHub Desktop](http://desktop.github.com).

### Adding Code to Git {#adding-code-to-git}

Open GitHub desktop, and click File \> New Repository… (Ctrl+N). Enter the details you’d like for the repository. Make sure that for the local path, you select the folder you have placed the XRP project into.

Git operates in ‘commits’. These are like checkpoints, or versions in the timeline. Every commit will save the state of every file, and can be undone or altered by subsequent commits. Create a commit by using the commit button in the bottom left, after filling in the title (and optionally the description) of the commit.

Once created, in the header bar, click push to origin. This will upload your code to GitHub. Make sure to get in the habit of doing this at the end of every practice. Otherwise, any robot code you may have written stays on your laptop, and is inaccessible to your teammates. Once you have done this, the bar should change to say ‘fetch origin’.

## DifferentialDrive  {#differentialdrive}

The DifferentialDrive object allows you to more easily convert from advanced movement to wheel speeds. It’s possible to implement things like arcade drive without the kinematics object using simple math, but it's more readable and concise to use it this way. The tech we’ll be using today is documented [on the FRC docs website](https://frcdocs.wpi.edu/en/2024/docs/software/hardware-apis/motors/wpi-drive-classes.html#using-the-differentialdrive-class-to-control-differential-drive-robots%20).

Today, you will be converting your robot code to use the DifferentialDrive object to control your drivetrain. I recommend creating a new command for this task, and simply modifying your subsystem.

# What is command-based programming? {#what-is-command-based-programming?}

*See Also: [What Is “Command-Based” Programming?](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/what-is-command-based.html)*

Command-based programming is a **design pattern** \- a way of structuring your code. It’s particularly effective, and used by most competitive FRC robotics teams. It also allows programmers to practice **declarative programming** \- that is *what to do*, not *how to do it*, making code more extensible and re-usable.

The command-based paradigm is based on two key abstractions, commands & subsystems:

* **Commands** are actions the robot can take. After command objects are constructed, they are scheduled to be **initialized**, before **updating** every 20ms. They will run until they are **finished** or interrupted, thus **ending**. Commands should do one simple task, so that they can be **composed** together
* **Subsystems** are mechanisms on the robot. They represent a collection of parts that can operate together \- whether that be by taking in data or executing a physical action.

Both of these are base classes you can create your own objects on top of.

## Running Commands {#running-commands}

Commands should never be run manually \- they are handled by the [**CommandScheduler**](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/command-scheduler.html), and can be run in parallel or sequence as long as there are no conflicts over what parts of the robot you require (ie you can't tell an arm to go up and down at the same time).

The command scheduler will execute a command once it is scheduled. In order to schedule a command, you must do one of the following:

* **Set the Default Command:** The command scheduler can have a ‘default’ command that runs while no other command overrides its behaviour. This is typically used to handle driving: since the autonomous commands require the drivetrain they override the default command which takes input from a Human Input Device.
* **Set the Autonomous Command:** At the beginning of the autonomous phase of the game, you are allowed to schedule an autonomous command which controls the robot for the first 15 seconds of the game.
* **Triggers:** This is the primary way to take input from the drivers and make the robot respond to it.

### On Triggers {#on-triggers}

*See Also: [Binding Commands to Triggers](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/binding-commands-to-triggers.html)*

Classes representing Human Input Devices have functions which produce trigger objects when called (trigger factories). For example, to get the trigger associated with the X button on an xbox controller you would use the following code:

```java
CommandXboxController exampleCommandController = new CommandXboxController(0);
Trigger xButton = exampleCommandController.x();

xButton.onTrue(() -> System.out.println("Hello World!"));
```

You can also make your own triggers. This trigger would fire when the endgame starts:

```java
Trigger endgameStarted = new Trigger(
    () -> DriverStation.isTeleopEnabled()
           && DriverStation.getMatchTime() > 0
           && DriverStation.getMatchTime() <= 20
);
```

## Command Compositions {#command-compositions}

*See Also: [Command Compositions](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/commandbased/command-compositions.html)*

Every command extends from the same base class, meaning they all have access to some utility functions allowing for commands to be chained together[^1]. The result of these are Command Compositions. They can be used to implement sequences of actions, or even some more complicated actions. They read pretty similar to english, see if you can figure out what the following does:

```java
endgameStarted.onTrue(new RumbleControllersCommand(0.5).withTimeout(0.5));
```

## Review {#review}

- [ ] **Commands** are classes that represent the actions a robot can take.
- [ ] **Subsystems** are classes that represent the mechanisms on a robot.
- [ ] Commands can be **triggered** by human input, or by the **CommandScheduler**.
- [ ] Commands can be chained together in **compositions**.

# Drivetrains {#drivetrains}

Before starting this section, you should have been assigned an XRP. Now, we will be getting our XRPs to handle basic movement. Documentation for the XRP is available on the [FRC docs website](https://frcdocs.wpi.edu/en/latest/docs/xrp-robot/index.html).

## Creating an FRC project {#creating-an-frc-project}

In VS Code, open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) and type “\>WPILib Create a new project”. This will open the project creation wizard. Make sure that you select “template \> java \> Command XRP”, other than that it’s not too important where you put your files or what your team number is as long as you can find it again.

When you open the new project, make sure to press “Trust Folder”. Then, add the project to git.

## The problem {#the-problem}

You are going to *create a subsystem to control the XRP’s drivetrain.* We will do so with command based programming principles. If you‘d like, take a moment to think about how to achieve this. We will be implementing a *tank drive*[^2], and for your self-guided task we will be creating an *arcade drive*. While completing this task, as always, please refrain from using generative AI tools and instead ask for help from your peers, a student leader, or mentor.

First, let’s map out the problem. In order to be able to tank drive the robot using a HID, we must:

1. Take input from a HID.
2. Use that input to update the Drivetrain subsystem’s state.
3. Apply the state changes made within the subsystem.

In order to get our robot moving, we need a couple more things:

* A way for the DriveTrain **subsystem** to receive speed requests.
* A way for the DriveTrain to *periodically process* those requests, and update the motors.
* A drive **command** to take input from a human input device[^3].

Let’s start by implementing a subsystem.

## The subsystem {#the-subsystem}

Now that you’ve created a new project for interfacing with the XRP, open the subsystems folder (“src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/”) and create a new file called Drivetrain.java. You may have an example drivetrain implementation \- you can look at this if you would like, but I’d recommend deleting this file to prevent confusion later.

Inside Drivetrain.java, we need to turn the generated class into a subsystem. All subsystems extend from SubsystemBase:

```java
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase;

public class Drivetrain extends SubsystemBase {
  // Subsystem implementation goes here
}
```


We also need to make sure the subsystem class has access to all parts of the physical Drivetrain \- in this case the left-hand motor and the right-hand motor.

```java
private final XRPMotor leftMotor = new XRPMotor(0);
private final XRPMotor rightMotor = new XRPMotor(1);
```

## The command {#the-command}

Open the file RobotContainer.java and add the following line:

```java
private final XboxController controller = new XboxController(0);
```

Now, we can access the state of the controller as we wish. Now, we need a way to process this. We will do this through a **command**.

Create a new file in the command folder called TankDrive.java. In order to process controller input, this command must do the following:

1. Store a reference to the HID & the DriveTrain
2. Periodically, use the state of the HID to update the state of the DriveTrain.

Put the following code in the TankDrive command:

```java
public class TankDrive extends Command {
  // These are our references to our controller and drivetrain.
  private final XboxController controller;
  private final DriveTrain drivetrain;

  public TankDrive(XboxController controller, DriveTrain drivetrain) {
    // The 'this' keyword indicates that we are refering to the FIELD (private final ...) named controller, and not the local variuble created by the constructor paramaters
  this.controller = controller;
  this.drivetrain = drivetrain;

  addRequirements(drivetrain);
}

@override
public void execute() {
  drivetrain.setMotors(controller.getLeftY(), controller.getRightY());
}
}
```

Here we get our first few function definitions. The constructor is a special function that runs the instant the object in instantiated (copied from the class definition using the new keyword). It has the same name as the class. We also get the periodic function. This function is run by the robot automatically 20 times a second, and in this case we use it to set the motor speeds on the drivetrain.

Now, using information we obtained last practice, and the example above, add a new function to the drivetrain called “setMotors” that takes two numbers and sets the speed of each motor when called.

Finally, to like this all together, go back to robot container and add the following code below the controller field:

```java
private final DriveTrain drivetrain = new Drivetrain();
```

And within the RobotContainer constructor add the following:

```java
drivetrain.setDefaultCommand(new TankDrive(controller, drivetrain));
```

This tells the drivetrain to run the tank drive command if nothing else is supposed to run on the drivetrain.

Once you’ve gotten your code done, let Aceius know, and they’ll grab a controller for you to test with.

## Review {#review-1}

- [ ] We created a subsystem to represent the drivetrain.
- [ ] We created a command to control the drivetrain.
- [ ] We scheduled that command by setting it as the drivetrain’s default command.

# Other Devices, HUDs {#other-devices,-huds}

Good evening. Today we will begin exploring the gyroscope, and how to display information to the driver.

## Gyroscopes {#gyroscopes}

Gyroscopes are devices used to measure and maintain orientation and angular velocity. They detect changes in rotational motion, allowing it to provide information about the orientation of an object in three-dimensional space. This is, for example, how your phone can tell when it is rotated.

On the competition robots, the gyro is used to help determine the location of the robot on the field, as well as used to calculate field relative drive inputs (where the heading of the robot is decoupled from the heading of the controls).

The XRPs have their own gyroscopes, which we will be learning about today

## Shuffleboard {#shuffleboard}

![][image4]

Shuffleboard is a system used to display information to the driver. Data on the shuffleboard can be viewed either through the Elastic app or Shuffleboard app, installed with FRC. During competitions, it can be used to display all sorts of useful data about the robot code’s state, such as current field position, or the state of a mechanism.

Our goal for today is to link the gyroscope to the shuffleboard dashboard, in order to display the robot’s current position.

## Writing Code {#writing-code}

I would recommend that you create a new subsystem for the gyro, but this is optional. You can also integrate it into your drivetrain class. Go ahead and create a new subsystem:

```java
// subsystems/Gyro.java
package frc.robot.subsystems;

public class Gyro extends SubsystemBase {
// gyro here

@Override

  // update smartdashboard
```

In order to get the gyro show the robot’s orientation on the dashboard, we need to:

1. Register the gyro in code
2. Read values from the gyroscope
3. Send said values to shuffleboard

The data type of the gyroscope is XRPGyro. Instantiate a new XRPGyro the same way you learned to create motors. Normally, a gyro would require a port number, but since only one gyroscope is on the XRP we can omit it here.

You can access the values using gyro.getAngleX(), gyro.getAngleY(), and gyro.getAngleZ().

Inside the periodic function, you can use the add function to display data. For example:

```java
Shuffleboard.getTab("SmartDashboard")
.add("Pi", 3.14);
```

The first argument of the add() function is always a ‘key’ string, or a name for the value. The second value can be any object, and it will be shown in the smart dashboard as text. Some values support custom display types however, which we will show later.

After feeding the getAngle values into the add() function, we should be able to see the values updating live on SmartDashboard.

One final nitpick is that the gyro will often report data with a great margin of error. To combat this we can filter the data using a median filter. These average the data inputting them, and return a filtered output.

Add the following field to your gyro class:

```java
// Creates a MedianFilter with a window size of 3 samples
private MedianFilter xFilter = new MedianFilter(3);
```

And then, instead of feeding gyro.getAngleX() to the smart dashboard, pass it xFilter.calculate(gyro.getAngleX()).

### Solution {#solution}

```java
package frc.robot.subsystems;

import edu.wpi.first.math.filter.MedianFilter;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.shuffleboard.Shuffleboard;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.shuffleboard.ShuffleboardTab;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.xrp.XRPGyro;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase;

public class Gyro extends SubsystemBase {
    private XRPGyro gyro;

    private MedianFilter xFilter = new MedianFilter(3);
    private MedianFilter yFilter = new MedianFilter(3);
    private MedianFilter zFilter = new MedianFilter(3);

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        ShuffleboardTab tab = Shuffleboard.getTab("SmartDashboard");

        tab.add("Gyro/AngleX", xFilter.calculate(gyro.getAngleX()));
        tab.add("Gyro/AngleY", yFilter.calculate(gyro.getAngleY()));
        tab.add("Gyro/AngleZ", zFilter.calculate(gyro.getAngleZ()));
    }
}
```

Good day. In this activity, we will learn about the Proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller, and its use in controlling outputs of systems.

# What is a PID Controller? {#what-is-a-pid-controller?}

A **PID controller** is a method that helps keep something steady, such as the speed or position of a motor. It works by adjusting its actions based on how far off the current state is from the desired target (the **setpoint**), as well as considering past errors and how quickly things are changing. This way, it ensures the system smoothly reaches and maintains the right level without wild swings or delays. It uses three values to calculate its output: Proportional, Integral, and Derivative.

## Uses {#uses}

Suppose that we have an [arm that must raise and lower to different](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1n60naaa9aWT73Z-7fcbAaE7eq8XNN99T/view?usp=sharing) [positions](http://positions.In). If we were to simply increase or decrease the power linearly, the arm might overshoot its destination, and wobble as it attempts to approach its target. In order to smoothly articulate the arm up and down, we can use a PID controller to control the amount of voltage sent to the arm.

### Example {#example}

Jessie is standing by the entrance of the arts center and wants to get to the Home of the Upper School entrance as quickly as possible. If she were to sprint as fast as she could in the direction of the HotUS entrance, she would arrive there very quickly, but then embarrassingly smack into the doors. A better solution would be for Jessie to quickly run towards the entrance and slow down right before approaching so she comes to a complete stop right at the desired point. This is her setpoint.

## Using a PID Controller on the XRP {#using-a-pid-controller-on-the-xrp}

A blank PID controller can be created in code by instantiating the [PIDController](https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/advanced-controls/controllers/pidcontroller.html) class. On the real robot, the PID controllers are built into a circuit on the hardware that are optimized just for PID calculations. This allows them to be as performant as possible. However, no such hardware exists on the XRP, hence the use of the software PID controller.

```java
// Creates a PIDController with gains kP, kI, and kD
PIDController pid = new PIDController(kP, kI, kD);
```

We’ll talk about the specifics of gains in just a moment, but for now let’s assume each constant is 0\. We now have a blank PID controller with neither a goal or any accumulated history. By calling the method calculate(), we can update the PID controller’s internal history and also tell it to move towards a setpoint.

# Style Guide {#style-guide}

## File Layout {#file-layout}

* Import statements
* Package statement
* Class
  * Constants
  * Fields
  * Constructor
  * Methods

## Comments {#comments}

* Always write javadoc documentation comments.
* Use `//` instead of `/* */` when writing comments.
* If you are doing something for a non-apparent reason, leave a comment.
* Avoid committing commented out code.

## Naming & Grammar {#naming-&-grammar}

* Types are `PascalCase.`
* ‘Constants’ should use uppercase `SNAKE_CASE`.
* Fields and local variables should use `camelCase`.
* **DO NOT ABBREVIATE NAMES.**
  * Mathematical operations (X, Y, Omega) are ok.
* Prefer Oxford comma.

## Blocks {#blocks}

* Always create blocks, even for single statements, unless inside a switch case.
* `{` on own line.
* `}` on own line unless followed by another closing character

## Leading Whitespace {#leading-whitespace}

* Use 4 spaces for indentation.
* Do not use raw multiline strings, because they break indentation.

## Functions {#functions}

* A function's entire signature should be on a single line.

## Variables {#variables}

* Use primitive types over Box types (for example, `nint` over `IntPtr`)
* Use static types. Do not use the `var` keyword.

## Keywords {#keywords}

* Use a space after `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` (they are not function calls).
* Do not use a space after the opening `(` and before the closing `)`.

## Handling Errors {#handling-errors}

* All methods must catch all possible exceptions. Do not throw exceptions.
* If it is possible that a method can fail, use the `Optional<T>` type as needed.


# Appendix A: Safety Protocol

# Robot Testing Safety Checklist

## Before Power

- [ ] Alert an adult supervisor to your presence & plans
- [ ] Ensure all personnel have eye protection
- [ ] Ensure the robot has no loose objects resting on or within it
- [ ] Secure the battery
- [ ] Attach bumpers to the robot
- [ ] Fortify the the area around the robot
      **– OR –**
      Ensure the robot is securely suspended above the ground

*You may now power the robot.*

## Before Enable

- [ ] Ensure all people are clear of the testing area
- [ ] Verify controllers connection integrity (if manually controlling the robot)
- [ ] Ensure all input devices are not caught on objects or otherwise stuck in their active state
- [ ] Clear the driver station area of objects hindering an E-Stop (emergency stop)
- [ ] Be ready to disable or E-Stop
- [ ] Loudly and clearly announce you are enabling the robot (“Enabling\!”)

*You may now enable the robot*

## During Operation

- [ ] Watch the robot at all times and be ready to disable or E-Stop

*Make sure to turn off the robot when you’re done with it\!*
